name: reese-hardstep-terrorist
idea: The lead is a growling, overdriven Reese bassline: two detuned saw-ish basses beating against each other in the low mids, moving in a slow menacing riff, the 1994 hardstep sound of Renegade's era. Under it, the classic Amen break thrashed at about 165 BPM, thick and heavy, barely chopped at first, then rolling. Ask for it in genre-and-era words (mid-90s hardstep turning into jump-up, dark, warehouse) and state plainly that there are no lead synths, no rave stabs, no pads and nothing high-pitched above the cymbals. It starts on the downbeat at full force, no intro.

name: ganja-dusty-jump-up
idea: Take the Ganja Records road: the lean, hip-hop-minded 1995 jump-up that writers call 'un-electronic'. The performer is a dusty, sampled funk drummer: a crackly vinyl Amen break chopped into cheeky, swaggering combinations, plus a short brassy funk horn stab or a fat bass guitar lick lifted off an old record. The bass is a bouncy, wobbling mid-range jump-up riff that makes a crowd skank, with dub-style space between hits. Ask for it through the record-collector mixdown: sampled off vinyl, lo-fi, punchy, swagger, bounce, playful menace. Nothing synthetic on top.

name: two-instruments-only
idea: Ask by subtraction and behaviour, never naming a subgenre: the whole track is only two things, a breakbeat and a sub. The break's behaviour is described in detail (rolling, ghost-heavy, snare rolls that skid, swerve and stutter, chopped edits every fourth bar, time-stretched metallic grain), while the sub is a deep sine that only answers the kick, leaving gaps so every drum hit reads. Include a clear space rule: everything above the hi-hats is empty, no melody, no chords, no synth, no pad. The feeling is a stripped dubplate cut for a sound system, relentless and loopable from bar one.

name: ragga-soundsystem-dub
idea: The lead voice is a heavy dub sound-system bassline, played like a reggae bass player's riff but at jungle speed, with tape echo and spring reverb throws on single snare hits. The Amen break runs underneath at 160-165 BPM, rolling and chopped, raw and saturated; the low end is a speaker-shaking 1995 ragga-jungle pressure, with a deep sub kick and a bass drop at the start. Ask for it as the music of a Brixton/Hackney sound-system dance in 1995: rumbling, dread, bass-heavy, dark and warm, with no siren, no airhorn, no vocal samples and no keys or synths, so all the energy lives in drums, bass and echo.
